title: System design

definition.text: System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements.

facts.text: System design meets the needs of a business or organization through coherent and efficient systems, and it takes a systematic approach to building and engineering them.
A good system design requires thinking about everything, from the infrastructure all the way down to the data and how it is stored.
The study of system design is the understanding of a system's component parts and how they interact with one another.
Designing the overall structure of a system aims at a scalable, reliable and efficient system.

Architecture design covers functional and non-functional requirements, relational or NoSQL databases, vertical and horizontal scaling, sharding, message queues, publish-subscribe, monitoring and logging, and build, test and deploy automation.
System design helps define a solution that meets the business requirements and is one of the earliest decisions made when building a system.
High-level design decisions are very difficult to correct later, so it is essential to think from a high level early on.
A clear design also makes it easier to reason about and manage architectural changes as the system evolves.

notes: Wikipedia's Systems design page is mostly product-development framing; the Physical design subsection (input/output, control, backup) was left out as off-topic for distributed systems.

definition.text: A system design interview evaluates a candidate's ability to produce technical solutions to abstract problems, so it has no single expected answer.

facts.text: System design is a very extensive topic, and interviews on it are not designed for one specific answer.
The interview is unusual because it is two-way between the candidate and the interviewer.

Expectations differ at each engineering level, because an experienced engineer approaches the problem differently from someone new, so it is hard to give one strategy that keeps every candidate organized.
System design interview questions are vague or abstract by nature.

A discussion checklist for interviews touches on load balancing, API gateway, communication protocols, CDN, message queue, unique ID generation, scalability, availability, performance, and fault tolerance and resilience.
Singh advises reading the engineering blog of the company you are interviewing with, to learn its technology stack and which problems matter to it.

title: System design interview framework

definition.text: A system design interview goes best when worked as a fixed sequence: clarify requirements, estimate capacity, design the high-level structure, the data and the interfaces, then address scale and reliability.

facts.text: Start by clarifying functional and non-functional requirements: ask about the core features and about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale.

Estimate capacity next: number of users, traffic, storage and memory needs, and compute and networking requirements. Useful questions are the desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed.
Define the data model early: the entities and the relationships between them, which shows the data flow at the core of every system. Then choose a database type and settle the schema.
Design the APIs as a simple interface of parameters, functions, classes, types and entities, without writing code. Keep it simple and revisit it when covering extended requirements.
Interfaces can be API endpoints or event models exchanged between components, with a communication approach such as REST, GraphQL, gRPC or event-driven.

Break the system into components such as client apps, servers, load balancers and databases. Draw a simple block diagram, focus on the data flow, then walk through how the system works from the client's perspective.
In the detailed design, pick with the interviewer the major components to go deeper on, such as data partitioning, load distribution, caching and handling a sudden traffic spike.
Finish with bottlenecks and reliability: ask whether there are enough database replicas, any single point of failure, a need for sharding, and how to make the system and its cache more robust.

notes: Order differs by source: ByteByteGo draws the high-level block diagram before database and interface design, Singh designs data model and API first. Facts follow Singh's order and add ByteByteGo's scalability step.

definition.text: Requirements clarification is asking early about the exact scope of an interview problem and sorting what the system must do into functional, non-functional and extended requirements.

facts.text: Because interview questions are vague, ask about the exact scope of the problem and clarify functional requirements early.
Requirements are usually divided into three parts: functional, non-functional and extended requirements.

Functional requirements are the basic functionalities the end user demands, all of which must be built into the system as part of the contract. Ask which features to design for and which edge cases to consider.

Non-functional requirements are quality constraints the system must satisfy, so ask about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale; for example every request needs minimum latency and the system should be highly available.
Extended requirements are nice-to-have items that may be out of scope, such as recording metrics and analytics or monitoring service health and performance.

definition.text: In the detailed design stage of an interview, present several approaches with their advantages and disadvantages, explain decisions with examples, and stay humble about what you know.

facts.text: Present different approaches with their advantages and disadvantages, and explain design decisions backed by examples; this is a good time to show expertise.
Avoid being too opinionated about technologies: a statement such as 'NoSQL databases are just better, SQL databases are not scalable' reflects poorly.
Singh advises being humble about what you know and do not know, and using existing knowledge with examples to navigate this part of the interview.

title: Machine learning systems design

definition.text: Machine learning systems design builds scalable, reliable and efficient systems that integrate machine learning models to solve real-world problems.

facts.text: ML systems need careful design of data pipelines, model training and deployment infrastructure, and are often used for recommendation engines, fraud detection and natural language processing.
Key components are problem definition (data requirements and evaluation metrics), a data pipeline, model selection and training, deployment and serving, and monitoring and maintenance.
Designing an ML system balances trade-offs between accuracy, latency, cost and maintainability, while keeping the system scalable and reliable.
The discipline overlaps with MLOps, practices that unify machine learning development and operations to ease deployment and lifecycle management.

notes: Likely off-syllabus for a course on distributed-systems interview questions; kept because it has its own section on the Systems design page.

title: System design building blocks

definition.text: The building blocks of system design are the standard components, grouped into six broad categories, that designs are assembled from.

facts.text: The building blocks fall into six broad categories: distributed computing, scalability and performance, service management, networking and communication, data storage and management, and observability and resiliency.

Distributed computing blocks are message queues, which allow async communication and decouple services; distributed caching, which keeps frequently accessed data in memory; and a task scheduler that coordinates running tasks.

Scalability and performance blocks are scaling services that adjust capacity to demand, CDNs that serve content from geographically closer locations, and consistent hashing that minimizes key remapping when nodes join or leave.
Service discovery lets services find and talk to each other without hard-coded network locations.

Networking blocks are DNS, which maps domain names to IP addresses; the load balancer, which spreads incoming traffic across servers; and the API gateway, a single entry point for a group of microservices.

Data storage blocks are databases for structured data, object storage for images, videos and documents, sharding to partition data across nodes, and replication to scale the database by copying data to multiple nodes.
Observability and resiliency means gaining insight into the system's internal state through metrics, logging and tracing.

notes: A ByteByteGo guide written to accompany a diagram; only its list sentences are cited. Each block has its own chapter elsewhere.

title: Common scaling problems and fixes

definition.text: Eight problems recur in large-scale production systems, and each has a standard remedy: caching, async workers, redundancy, load balancing, CDNs, object storage, central logging and database indexing or sharding.

facts.text: A read-heavy system is helped by caching to make reads faster.
High write traffic is handled with async workers that process the writes, or with databases powered by LSM-trees.
A single point of failure is removed by redundancy and failover mechanisms for critical components such as databases.
For high availability, use load balancing so that requests go to healthy server instances, and database replication to improve durability and availability.
High latency is reduced with a content delivery network.
Large files and complex data are handled with block storage and object storage.
Monitoring and alerting use a centralized logging system, for example the ELK stack.
Slower database queries are fixed with proper indexes and by sharding to scale the database horizontally.

notes: A one-line-per-problem list from a ByteByteGo guide; the problem headings carry the pairing.

title: Software architecture

definition.text: Software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system, and the discipline of creating them.

facts.text: Each architectural structure comprises software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both the elements and the relations.
The architecture works as the blueprints for the system and the development project, and it is about fundamental structural choices that are costly to change once implemented.

Application design covers the processes and data behind the required functionality, while architecture design shapes the infrastructure in which that functionality runs so that the system's non-functional requirements are met.
Architecture is design but not all design is architectural; in practice the architect draws the line between architectural design and detailed design, and no rule fits all cases.
Two fundamental laws of software architecture are that everything is a trade-off and that why is more important than how.
Software architectures fall into two main types, monolith and distributed architecture, and tend to become more complex over time.

As an intellectually graspable abstraction, architecture lets teams analyse a system's behavior before it is built, saving cost and risk, and lets stakeholders discuss design decisions while they are still relatively easy to adapt.
Conway's observation is that organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures; Fred Brooks popularized it as Conway's Law.

notes: Wikipedia's Software architecture page covers general (not only distributed) software; sections on Mozilla's erosion case, ATAM/TARA frameworks and agile big-design-up-front were left out.

title: Non-functional requirements

definition.text: A non-functional requirement specifies criteria for judging how a system operates, an overall property such as availability or performance, rather than a specific behavior.

facts.text: Broadly, functional requirements define what a system is supposed to do and non-functional requirements define how it is supposed to be: they take the form 'system shall be <requirement>', an overall property rather than a specific function.

It is important to specify non-functional requirements in a specific and measurable way, because a system's overall properties commonly mark the difference between a development project succeeding or failing.

They are also called quality attributes, qualities, quality goals, quality of service requirements or constraints, informally the 'ilities', and in software architecture 'architectural characteristics'; some call them cross-functional requirements.

Qualities fall into two categories: execution qualities such as safety, security and usability are observable at run time, while evolution qualities such as testability, maintainability, extensibility and scalability are embodied in the static structure of the system.

Typical examples are availability, performance (speed, throughput, response time), reliability (mean time between failures), maintainability (mean time to repair), fault tolerance and resource constraints such as memory, disk space and network bandwidth.

A system may have to display the number of records in a database: how current that number must be is a non-functional requirement, and real-time updating obliges architects to keep the display within an acceptably short interval of the change.

In an interview, non-functional requirements sound like 'each request should be processed with the minimum latency' and 'the system should be highly available', next to portability, maintainability, reliability, scalability and security.

Non-functional requirements are usually architecturally significant, so their plan is detailed in the system architecture, which is tied more closely to quality attributes than to functionality; the architect must match these characteristics with business requirements.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry (built from Singh and Software architecture) now that the Wikipedia page is crawled. The ISO/IEC 25010 qualities, the business-driver to quality mapping, the 'cross-functional' criticism and the per-microservice characteristics are kept only as mentions.

definition.text: An architecture pattern is a reusable, proven solution to a recurring system-level problem, and an architecture style is a high-level structural organization of a system.

facts.text: A software architecture pattern is a reusable, proven solution to a recurring system-level problem about overall structure, component interactions and quality attributes, at a higher level of abstraction than software design patterns.

An architecture style is a high-level structural organization that says how components are organized, how they interact and what constrains those interactions, using a vocabulary of component and connector types.
Styles are the most coarse-grained level of system organization, for example layered architecture, microservices, event-driven architecture and hexagonal architecture.
The distinction between architectural patterns and styles can sometimes be blurry; common terms for recurring solutions also include tactic and reference architecture.

definition.text: Software architecture design consists of four core activities, analysis, synthesis, evaluation and evolution, carried out iteratively.

facts.text: Four core activities make up architecture design and are performed iteratively, at different stages of initial development and over the system's evolution.

Architectural analysis understands the environment of a proposed system and determines its requirements; its outputs are the architecturally significant requirements, those with a measurable impact on the architecture.

Synthesis creates and improves the design from the architecturally significant requirements, and evaluation determines how well the current design satisfies them, for example with the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM).

Evolution maintains and adapts an existing architecture to changing requirements and environment, while supporting activities run throughout: knowledge management and communication, design reasoning and decision-making, and documentation.

definition.text: Architecture decision records are single, accessible records that capture each architectural decision with its technical and business justification.

facts.text: Making an architectural decision involves collecting enough information, justifying the decision, documenting it with its rationale, and communicating it to the right stakeholders; the architecture includes these decisions, not only models.
Fear of choosing wrongly can make an architect delay decisions; close collaboration with the development team and deciding at the 'last responsible moment' avoids analysis paralysis.
Forgotten, undocumented or misunderstood decisions, often those communicated by email, cause repeated discussions without resolution.

Architects usually record both technical and business justification, often about cost, user satisfaction and time to market, in one Architecture Decision Record kept in an accessible repository such as a wiki, so there is a single updated source of truth.

title: Software architecture erosion

definition.text: Software architecture erosion is a gradual gap that opens over time between a system's intended and implemented architecture.

facts.text: Erosion may occur at any stage of the software development life cycle and affects development speed and maintenance cost.

It is caused by architectural violations, accumulating technical debt and knowledge vaporization, and it can decrease performance, substantially increase evolutionary costs and degrade software quality.

Preventative measures include enforcing architectural rules, regular code reviews and automated testing; remedial measures include refactoring, redesign and documentation updates; conformance checks and static analysis help detect erosion early.
Architecture recovery uncovers a system's architecture from its implementation and documentation, and is often needed when documentation is out of date or the architecture has eroded.

title: Requirements engineering

definition.text: Requirements engineering is the work of eliciting, analysing, specifying, validating and managing what a system must do, the 'what' that architecture answers with a 'how'.

facts.text: Requirements engineering addresses the problem space, the 'what', while software architecture targets the solution space, the 'how'; the two are complementary approaches.

Its activities are elicitation of stakeholders' needs, analysis and negotiation to resolve conflicts, specification in a requirements specification, validation that the documents are consistent and meet needs, and management of changes throughout.

The waterfall model makes it the first phase of development, but later methods such as the Rational Unified Process assume it continues through a system's lifetime, and its activities interleave in practice rather than running in strict stages.
Required behavior impacts the solution architecture, which in turn may introduce new requirements; the Twin Peaks model aims to exploit this relation.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry (built from the Software architecture section only) now that the Wikipedia page is crawled. The old fact on the overlap of the two fields and the page's Issues section are kept only as mentions.

definition.text: A functional requirement defines a function of a system or component as behavior between inputs and outputs, a statement of what the system is supposed to accomplish.

facts.text: Functional requirements may involve calculations, technical details, data manipulation and processing and other specific functionality, and are usually written 'system shall do <requirement>' for one individual action or part of the system.

Functional requirements drive the application architecture of a system, while non-functional requirements drive its technical architecture; functional requirements are planned in the system design, non-functional ones in the system architecture.

Behavioral requirements describe the cases where the system uses the functional requirements and are captured in use cases; an analyst may derive functional requirements from a set of use cases, or write the use cases after gathering the requirements.
A specification has a unique name and number, a brief summary, a rationale, the required behavior and references to related use cases; the crux is a clear, readable description of the behavior.

title: Software design pattern

definition.text: A software design pattern is a reusable template for solving a commonly needed behavior in software, usable across programming languages and platforms.

facts.text: A design pattern is not a rigid structure to copy into source code but a template for a type of problem; it works below architecture patterns, which solve broader system-level challenges.
Reusing proven patterns speeds up development, helps prevent hidden, subtle issues that fresh code can carry, and makes code more readable to those who know the patterns.
Patterns are grouped by the kind of problem they solve: creational (factory method, builder), structural (adapter, decorator), behavioral (chain of responsibility, command) and concurrency patterns.

Critics say a need for a pattern may signal a missing language feature, since 16 of the 23 Design Patterns patterns are simplified or eliminated in Lisp or Dylan, and inappropriate use may needlessly increase complexity.

notes: History, the Gang of Four publication story, domain-specific patterns and the long pattern catalogs were left out as off-topic for a system-design course.

title: Conway's law

definition.text: Conway's law says that the structure of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organization that designs it.

facts.text: Organizations that design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures, because the authors of a product's parts must communicate to keep them compatible, so the technical structure reflects the organization's social boundaries.

The law is applied mainly in software architecture; strictly it describes a correspondence, not a cause, and commentators differ on whether design drives the organization, the organization drives design, or both, and on whether mirroring is desirable.

MIT and Harvard Business School researchers found strong evidence for the mirroring hypothesis: the product from the loosely-coupled organization was significantly more modular than the product from the tightly-coupled organization.

Coplien and Harrison advise making the organization compatible with the product architecture, since a project is in trouble when teams do not reflect the product's essential parts; Yourdon and Constantine call the two isomorphic.

notes: Its coining in 1967, the colloquial and humorous uses and the usability-of-websites example were left out as trivia.
